questions.question: In the ideal brute-force model, roughly how many trials does it take to search a k-bit key space?
questions.explanation: A k-bit key space has 2^k keys, so unstructured brute force scales like 2^k up to constant factors.

questions.question: What is the headline scaling change Grover's algorithm gives for unstructured search?
options: It turns 2^k work into about 2^(k/2) oracle queries
It turns 2^k work into about k oracle queries
It turns k work into about 2^k oracle queries
It turns 2^(k/2) work into about 2^k oracle queries
questions.explanation: Grover provides a quadratic speedup: the exponent is halved for idealized unstructured search.

questions.question: Ignoring constants and parallelism, what is Grover's log2(work) for searching an AES-256 key?
questions.explanation: Grover key search scales like 2^(k/2), so AES-256 corresponds to ~256/2 = 128 bits in this model.

questions.question: If you want ~128 bits of post-quantum strength against key search, which standard AES key size matches the simple Grover rule-of-thumb?
options: Any AES key size is equivalent under Grover
questions.explanation: To get ~128 Grover bits you need ~256 key bits, so AES-256 is the standard match.

questions.question: For an ideal n-bit hash, what is the classical log2(work) to find a collision (birthday bound)?
questions.explanation: Classical collision search scales like ~2^(n/2), so log2(work) is about n/2.

questions.question: For an ideal n-bit hash, what is the quantum log2(work) to find a collision under the BHT model?
questions.explanation: The BHT collision algorithm gives a ~2^(n/3) scaling for idealized collision finding.

questions.question: You model Grover key search as ~2^(k/2) queries. If an attacker has P = 2^20 identical quantum workers and can parallelize perfectly, how does log2(work) change?
options: It is unchanged because Grover can't be parallelized
questions.explanation: If work divides linearly by P, then log2(work/P) = log2(work) - log2(P) = log2(work) - 20.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the lesson's recommended mental model for 'security bits' under quantum?
options: State an attack model, compute log2(work), then adjust exponents (k -> k/2 for Grover) rather than making binary claims
Assume quantum instantly breaks all symmetric primitives, so always replace them with new ones
Ignore quantum for symmetric crypto because Grover is only theoretical
Treat '128-bit security' as a wall-clock guarantee independent of assumptions
questions.explanation: The lesson uses log2(work) as a model and updates it under Grover/BHT scaling, with explicit assumptions and caveats.
